title: OSWorld 2.0: Long-Horizon Computer Use, Stress-Tested
hook: 108 realistic computer-use workflows averaging 1.6 human-hours each expose how far agents are from professional-grade computer use — the best model completes only 20.6%.
key_points: Tasks average 318 tool calls each (versus ~30 in OSWorld 1.0), spanning streaming interaction, dynamic environments, and hidden state.
Claude Opus 4.8 tops out at 20.6% full completion (54.8% partial); GPT-5.5 plateaus near 13% but is far more token-efficient.
Agents don't fail at basic GUI control — they lose track of constraints, miss mid-task information, guess instead of asking, and skip verification.
Tasks are grounded in authentic artifacts and stateful user profiles, with separate safety audits for sensitive actions.
content_html: Computer-use agents look impressive on short demo tasks. OSWorld 2.0 asks what happens when the task takes a human 1.6 hours and hundreds of steps — and the answer is: agents are still far from ready.
extra_html: The benchmark introduces 108 long-horizon workflows across everyday and professional computer use, each requiring an average of 318 tool calls with Claude Opus 4.7 at maximum thinking — over ten times the roughly 30 calls OSWorld 1.0 tasks needed. Tasks target challenges prior benchmarks underrepresent: streaming interaction, dynamic environments, cross-source reasoning, implicit-state inference, and visual-spatial precision, all grounded in authentic artifacts and realistic stateful user profiles, with separate safety audits for sensitive actions. Under the primary binary-completion metric at 500 steps, the strongest agent — Claude Opus 4.8 with maximum thinking and batched tool calls — completes only 20.6% of tasks fully (54.8% partial), while GPT-5.5 is far more token-efficient but plateaus near 13%. The failure modes are telling: agents rarely stumble on basic GUI control or coding. They lose track of constraints, miss information that arrives mid-task, guess rather than ask the user, and skip verification — struggling most when a task hinges on hidden state they must recover themselves. Mengqi Yuan and colleagues, arXiv 2026.

related.title: Computer Use in Gemini 3.5 Flash
related.hook: DeepMind put computer-use agents — reading the screen, then clicking, typing, and scrolling through real UIs — into its fast, low-cost Flash tier.

related.title: GUI vs. CLI: Where Computer-Use Agents Get Stuck
related.hook: Should an agent click buttons or type commands? A matched benchmark giving both the same 440 tasks finds GUI agents win by default — but CLI agents leap ahead once their skill library is filled in.

related.title: TUA-Bench: Benchmarking General-Purpose Terminal Agents
related.hook: 120 real terminal tasks — from email triage to PhD-level scientific workflows — show even Claude Opus 4.8 tops out around 66%, far from reliable general computer use.

related.title: DocOps: Benchmarking Agents That Edit Real Documents
related.hook: Even frontier agents can't reliably edit complex documents: a verifiable benchmark pins the failures on three modes — state-tracking collapse, shallow verification, and destructive metadata edits.

flashcards.prompt: Where does the paper say agents actually fail on long-horizon computer-use tasks?

choices.text: Losing track of constraints, missing mid-task information, guessing instead of asking, and skipping verification
Basic mouse and keyboard control, which they cannot perform at all
Rendering the screen, which is too slow to be usable

flashcards.explanation_html: The bottleneck isn't low-level GUI control — it's higher-level planning and information management over long, realistic workflows.
